name: Davunetide
status: Investigational; failed a phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy; now being pursued for ADNP syndrome
mechanism: An eight-amino-acid piece of the brain protein ADNP that interacts with microtubule-tracking proteins, supporting the nerve cell skeleton and tau

article.summary: Davunetide (NAP) is an experimental nasal-spray peptide from the brain protein ADNP. It failed in progressive supranuclear palsy and is now aimed at ADNP syndrome.
article.takeaway: Davunetide is a short peptide copied from activity-dependent neuroprotective protein (ADNP), a protein brain cells need for normal development. In the lab it helps stabilize microtubules, the internal scaffolding of nerve cells, and limits abnormal tau.[^1] Despite that promise, a one-year trial in 313 people with **progressive supranuclear palsy** found no benefit,[^2] and earlier studies in memory problems and schizophrenia gave mixed signals.[^3] Its developers now hope to treat **ADNP syndrome**, a rare genetic cause of autism and intellectual disability, but as of October 2026 no trial for that use appeared on ClinicalTrials.gov.
glance: PSP, mild cognitive impairment, schizophrenia; ADNP syndrome planned
Several phase 2 trials and one negative phase 2/3 trial
FDA orphan drug and rare pediatric disease designations for ADNP syndrome

blocks.text: ADNP was discovered at Tel Aviv University as a protein that nerve cells make when they are active and that protects them from damage. Its active core is an eight-amino-acid stretch, NAPVSIPQ, which became the drug candidate NAP and later davunetide.[^4]

Microtubules are hollow protein tubes that give nerve cells their shape and carry cargo along axons. Tau protein normally helps hold them steady; in diseases called tauopathies, tau detaches and clumps. Davunetide binds end-binding proteins that sit on the growing tips of microtubules, and in preclinical studies it supported microtubule stability, axonal transport and lower tau phosphorylation.[^1][^2] That made tauopathies such as progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) its first major target.

rows: Possible memory effects at some time points; not published in full[^5]
No effect on cognitive tests; better functional-skills scores[^3]
No registered trial found as of October 2026

blocks.text: The original developer, Allon Therapeutics, became insolvent after the PSP failure. Davunetide has since been licensed by a new company from Tel Aviv University and holds FDA orphan drug and rare pediatric disease designations, plus EU orphan status, for ADNP syndrome.[^5]

The PSP trial randomized 313 people to 30 mg of nasal davunetide twice daily or placebo for a year at 48 centers. Neither main measure, a PSP rating scale and an activities-of-daily-living scale, differed between groups.[^2] A 2023 re-analysis by the drug's inventors reported slower decline in women on davunetide, but such after-the-fact subgroup findings often fail to hold up and would need a new trial.[^6]

In ADNP syndrome, mutations in one copy of the ADNP gene cause developmental delay, autism features and other problems. The rationale for davunetide is to replace some of the lost protein's activity, and mouse models carrying ADNP mutations improved with NAP.[^7] No human efficacy data exist yet for this use.

Across trials in adults, nasal davunetide was generally well tolerated. The schizophrenia study reported no significant side effects,[^3] and headache and nasal irritation were the main complaints in the memory study.[^5] Safety in children, the group now being targeted, has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies.
Davunetide also appears on some research-peptide websites. Those products are not approved, and nothing supports using them for memory or brain health.

The licensing company has said a pediatric trial in ADNP syndrome began in 2024, but independent trackers could not find it in trial registries.[^5] Until a registered, controlled trial reports, davunetide remains an unproven idea for ADNP syndrome and a failed one for PSP.

evidence.label: Mixed: human trials, mostly negative
evidence.text: Davunetide has been tested in several randomized trials, but the largest, in PSP, was clearly negative,[^2] and smaller studies produced inconsistent results.[^3] Support for its newest target, ADNP syndrome, comes from laboratory and animal work.[^7]

faq.q: Is davunetide approved for any condition?
faq.a: No. It is not approved by the FDA or any other major regulator.

faq.q: Why did it fail in progressive supranuclear palsy?
faq.a: The reasons are unclear. Preventing tau damage in animals has not translated into benefit for people with PSP for several drugs, possibly because treatment starts too late or the target is not the main driver of disease.[^2]
Also called Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, it is a rare genetic condition caused by changes in the ADNP gene that leads to developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism features.[^7]
